awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Efficient Transfer Technology for Ultra-Thin Dies (UTD) in Advanced Semiconductor Chip Packaging
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial impacts of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase-I project is in increasing the USA footprint in the advanced semiconductor chip assembly and package equipment market.  The Ultra-thin die (UTD) semiconductor chip devices are building blocks for a wide range of mobile and flexible electronics applications.  These UTD chips are very fragile and their handling during manufacturing is substantially different from traditional chips.  The handling and transfer of UTD chips is a major contributor to the package cost and yield, which are critical for new technologies. In this project, an innovative technology will be developed for fast and precise transfer of UTD chips during semiconductor chip manufacturing. Customers for this technology are the world-wide original device manufacturers and semiconductor foundries, for use in a wide range of consumer products.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase-I project focuses on the introduction of a transfer technology capable of collectively transferring UTDs from the dicing tape to another substrate without the risk for die cracking, chipping or warpage. The “one-die-at-a-time” vacuum-based transfer that dominates today’s equipment market utilizes vacuum and a needle to push the die away from the tape while the pickup tool lifts the die off of the needle and places it into the appropriate output carrier.  This technology is a major contributor to die stress and cracking, especially for UTDs. As high-performance chips trend to increase in area and decrease in thickness (< 50 microns), the task of reliable peeling of UTDs from the dicing tape becomes more challenging. To address this challenge, this project introduces two innovative methodologies / hardware components; the first of which is a Vacuum-Activated, Patterned Stage (VAPS) essential for initiating the collective delamination of all dice placed on a UV-sensitive dicing tape substrate, while the second is a pattern-sensitive individually addressable head for the electromagnetic pick and place of released dice.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Ultra-thin dice (UTDs), typically less than 50 microns thick, are emerging as essential building blocks in semiconductor manufacturing. They offer significant benefits for AI hardware by enabling higher integration density in 3D ICs and system-in-package (SiP) designs. Despite the huge potential of UTDs, its sort, assembly and packaging remain extremely challenging. The outcome of this SBIR project demonstrated the proof-of-principle (PoP) behind the operation of LuxNour innovative VAPS (Vacuum-Assisted Patterned Stage) and magnetic-based pick-up head (PUH) chip transfer technology, as an enabling alternative to the standard needle-vacuum pick-and-place (PnP), which dominates the industry today. During the project, single die VAPS and PUH, as well as their equivalent for 150mm and 300mm diced wafer substrates, were designed, built and tested. The PoP behind VAPS operation was demonstrated on single die of both 600 microns and ultra-thin (30 microns) thickness using magnetic PUH and/or vacuum. On the other hand, experiments concluded the unsuitability of the collective VAPS transfer for dies without magnetic materials due to the uncontrolled vacuum leakage resulting from the inherent non-uniformity of the diced substrate. One undergraduate mechanical engineering student worked on the project as a technician and benefited from the team’s interactions, technical discussions and problem solving skills.

Extensive customer inquiry further supported the commercialization prospects of the VAPS technology over a wide range of die thickness (600 microns-100 microns), in addition to its unique effective solution for the unserved market for the UTD (30 microns). Therefore, the commercialization of LuxNour VAPS transfer technology directly increases the USA footprint in the advanced assembly package equipment market and may enhance the chances for the USA to compete in that space. In addition, the commercialization of the technology will enable the commercial utilization of UTD in a wide range of consumer products that improve the quality of life for people around the globe, including products based on flexible electronics, multi-chips and chips designed for parallel processing (like AI-chips).
